title: Book 1, Chapter 2 — Causes of the War—The Affair of Epidamnus—The Affair of Potidæa
paragraphs: The city of Epidamnus stands on the right at the entrance to the Ionic Gulf. The country around it is inhabited by the Taulantians, an Illyrian people. The city is a colony of Corcyra, founded by Phalius, son of Eratocleides, of the Heraclid family. As ancient custom required, he had been summoned for the purpose from Corinth, the mother country. The colonists were joined by some Corinthians and other Dorians. As time went on, Epidamnus grew large and populous; but it fell prey to internal factions, said to have arisen from a war with its barbarian neighbours, and was greatly weakened, losing much of its power. The final act before the war was the people’s expulsion of the nobles. The exiles joined the barbarians and began plundering the city by sea and land. Hard-pressed, the Epidamnians sent ambassadors to Corcyra, begging the mother country not to let them perish, but to settle matters between them and the exiles, and to free them from the war with the barbarians. The ambassadors took their seats as suppliants in the temple of Hera and made these requests of the Corcyraeans. But the Corcyraeans refused their supplication and dismissed them empty-handed.

When the Epidamnians found that no help could be expected from Corcyra, they did not know what to do next. So they sent to Delphi and asked the god whether they should hand over their city to the Corinthians and try to obtain some assistance from their founders. The god answered that they should hand over the city and place themselves under Corinthian protection. The Epidamnians went to Corinth and surrendered the colony in obedience to the oracle. They pointed out that their founder had come from Corinth, repeated the god’s answer, and begged the Corinthians not to let them perish but to assist them. The Corinthians agreed. They believed the colony belonged as much to themselves as to the Corcyraeans, and they felt a kind of duty to take its protection in hand. Besides, they hated the Corcyraeans for the contempt they showed the mother country. Other colonies honoured Corinth at public assemblies in the usual ways—precedence at sacrifices, for instance—but Corcyra treated her with contempt. And Corcyra was wealthy enough to stand comparison with the richest communities in Hellas, militarily strong, and at times openly proud of her naval reputation, which dated back to her old inhabitants, the Phaeacians. This was one reason the Corcyraeans took such care of their fleet, which became very efficient: they began the war with a force of one hundred and twenty galleys.

All these grievances made Corinth eager to send the promised aid to Epidamnus. A call went out for volunteer settlers, and a force of Ambraciots, Leucadians, and Corinthians was dispatched. They marched by land to Apollonia, a Corinthian colony, avoiding the sea route for fear of Corcyraean interference. When the Corcyraeans heard that settlers and troops had reached Epidamnus and that the colony had been surrendered to Corinth, they took fire. They put to sea at once with twenty-five ships, soon followed by more, and insolently ordered the Epidamnians to take back the banished nobles—(it must be noted that the Epidamnian exiles had gone to Corcyra and, pointing to the tombs of their ancestors, had appealed to their kinsmen to restore them)—and to dismiss the Corinthian garrison and settlers. But the Epidamnians turned a deaf ear to all of this. The Corcyraeans then began operations against them with a fleet of forty sail. They brought the exiles along with a view to restoring them, and also enlisted the help of the Illyrians. Sitting down before the city, they issued a proclamation: any of the natives who wished, and the foreigners, could leave unharmed; otherwise they would be treated as enemies. When this was refused, the Corcyraeans laid siege to the city, which stands on an isthmus. The Corinthians, hearing that Epidamnus was under blockade, gathered an expedition and proclaimed a colony to Epidamnus, with full political equality guaranteed to all who chose to go. Anyone not ready to sail at once could pay fifty Corinthian drachmae and have a share in the colony without leaving Corinth. Many took up the offer, some ready to sail immediately, others paying the fee. In case the Corcyraeans contested their passage, several cities were asked for a convoy. Megara prepared eight ships, Pale in Cephallonia four, Epidaurus five, Hermione one, Troezen two, Leucas ten, and Ambracia eight. The Thebans and Phliasians were asked for money, the Eleans for hulls as well; Corinth herself furnished thirty ships and three thousand heavy infantry.

When the Corcyraeans heard of these preparations, they came to Corinth with envoys from Lacedaemon and Sicyon, whom they had persuaded to accompany them. They told Corinth to recall the garrison and settlers, since she had no business in Epidamnus. If, however, she had any claims to make, they were willing to submit the matter to arbitration by Peloponnesian cities chosen by mutual agreement, and the colony would remain with whichever city the arbitrators assigned it to. They were also willing to refer the matter to the oracle at Delphi. If Corinth defied their protest and went to war, they themselves would be forced by this violence to seek friends in places they had no wish to seek them, and to set aside old ties out of necessity. Corinth answered that if the Corcyraeans would withdraw their fleet and the barbarians from Epidamnus, negotiation might be possible; but while the town was still under siege, arbitration was out of the question. The Corcyraeans replied that if Corinth would withdraw her troops from Epidamnus, they would withdraw theirs—or both sides could remain in place under an armistice until judgment could be given.

Turning a deaf ear to all these proposals, the Corinthians—their ships manned and their allies arrived—sent a herald ahead to declare war and put to sea with seventy-five ships and two thousand heavy infantry, sailing for Epidamnus to give battle to the Corcyraeans. The fleet was commanded by Aristeus, son of Pellichas, Callicrates, son of Callias, and Timanor, son of Timanthes; the troops by Archetimus, son of Eurytimus, and Isarchidas, son of Isarchus. When they reached Actium, in the territory of Anactorium, at the mouth of the Gulf of Ambracia where the temple of Apollo stands, the Corcyraeans sent ahead a herald in a light boat to warn them not to sail against them. Meanwhile the Corcyraeans manned their ships, all of them equipped for action, the older vessels girded with cables to keep them seaworthy. When the herald returned without any peaceful answer from the Corinthians, their ships now manned, they put out to sea to meet the enemy with a fleet of eighty sail (the other forty were engaged in the siege of Epidamnus), formed line, and went into battle. They won decisively, destroying fifteen Corinthian vessels. That same day Epidamnus was forced by its besiegers to capitulate; the terms were that the foreigners be sold and the Corinthians held as prisoners of war until their fate could be otherwise decided.

After the engagement the Corcyraeans set up a trophy on Leukimme, a headland of Corcyra, and put all their captives to death except the Corinthians, whom they kept as prisoners of war. Defeated at sea, the Corinthians and their allies returned home, leaving the Corcyraeans masters of all the seas in those parts. Sailing to Leucas, a Corinthian colony, they ravaged its territory and burned Cyllene, the harbour of the Eleans, because the Eleans had supplied Corinth with ships and money. For almost the entire period after the battle they remained masters of the sea, and Corinth’s allies were harassed by Corcyraean cruisers. At last Corinth, stirred by the suffering of her allies, sent out ships and troops in late summer. They formed an encampment at Actium and around Chimerium in Thesprotis to protect Leucas and the rest of the friendly cities. The Corcyraeans, on their side, set up a similar station at Leukimme. Neither side made any move; they remained facing each other until the end of summer, and winter was at hand before either of them returned home.

Corinth, exasperated by the war with the Corcyraeans, spent the entire year after the engagement and the next building ships and straining every nerve to form an effective fleet. Rowers were drawn from the Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas with the inducement of large bounties. The Corcyraeans, alarmed at the news of these preparations, were without a single ally in Hellas (they had not enrolled themselves in either the Athenian or Lacedaemonian confederacy), and decided to go to Athens to enter into alliance and try to obtain her support. Corinth, hearing of their intentions, also sent an embassy to Athens to prevent the Corcyraean navy from being joined by the Athenian, which would block her chance to conduct the war on her own terms. An assembly was convened, and the rival advocates appeared. The Corcyraeans spoke as follows:

“Athenians! When a people that has rendered no important service or support to its neighbours in the past, for which it might claim repayment, appears before them—as we now appear before you—to ask for assistance, they may fairly be required to satisfy certain preliminary conditions. They should show, first, that it is expedient or at least safe to grant their request; next, that they will retain a lasting sense of the kindness. If they cannot clearly establish either of these points, they must not be annoyed if they meet with refusal. Now the Corcyraeans believe that, along with their petition for help, they can give you a satisfactory answer on these points, and so have sent us here. Our policy with respect to this request happens to be inconsistent with our past, and at the present crisis inexpedient for our interests. We say inconsistent, because a power that throughout her history has been unwilling to ally with any of her neighbours is now found asking them to ally themselves with her. And we say inexpedient, because in our present war with Corinth that policy has left us in total isolation. What once seemed the wise precaution of refusing alliances—lest we be drawn into risks of others’ choosing—has now proved to be folly and weakness. It is true that in the recent naval engagement we drove the Corinthians back from our shores single-handed. But they have now gathered a still larger armament from the Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas. Seeing our utter inability to cope with them without foreign aid, and the magnitude of the danger that subjection to them implies, we must ask help from you and from every other power. We hope you will excuse us if we forswear our old principle of complete political isolation, a principle adopted with no sinister intention but rather as the consequence of an error in judgment.

“There are many reasons why, if you comply, you will congratulate yourselves on this request having been made to you. First, your assistance will be rendered to a power which, though herself inoffensive, is the victim of the injustice of others. Second, all that we most value is at stake in the present contest, and your welcoming us under these circumstances will be a proof of goodwill that will keep alive the gratitude we lay up in our hearts forever. Third, yourselves excepted, we are the greatest naval power in Hellas. Moreover, can you imagine a stroke of good fortune more rare in itself, or more disheartening to your enemies, than that the power whose adhesion you would have valued above much material and moral strength should present herself uninvited, deliver herself into your hands without danger and without expense, and finally put you in the way of gaining a high reputation in the eyes of the world, the gratitude of those whom you assist, and a great accession of strength for yourselves? You may search all history without finding many cases of a people gaining all these advantages at once, or many cases of a power that comes seeking aid being in a position to give the people whose alliance she solicits as much safety and honour as she will receive. But it will be objected that we shall be useful only in the case of a war. To this we answer: any of you who imagines that war is far off is gravely mistaken, and is blind to the fact that Lacedaemon eyes you with jealousy and wants war, that Corinth is powerful there—the same Corinth, remember, that is your enemy and is even now trying to subdue us as a preliminary to attacking you. She does this to keep us from being united against her by a common enmity, to avoid having us both on her hands at once, and also to gain the start on you in one of two ways—by crippling our power or by making its strength her own. Our policy must be to be beforehand with her: for Corcyra to make an offer of alliance, and for you to accept it. We ought to be making plans against her, not waiting to defeat the plans she makes against us.

“If she argues that it is not right for you to receive a colony of hers into alliance, let her know that every colony that is well treated honours its parent state, but is estranged from it by injustice. For colonists are not sent out to be the slaves of those who remain behind, but to be their equals. And it is clear that Corinth was injuring us. Invited to refer the dispute about Epidamnus to arbitration, she chose to prosecute her complaints by war rather than by a fair trial. Let her conduct toward us, who are her kindred, warn you not to be misled by her deceit, nor to give in to her direct requests; concessions to adversaries only end in self-reproach, and the more strictly they are avoided the better the chance of security.

“If it is urged that receiving us would be a breach of the treaty between you and Lacedaemon, the answer is that we are a neutral state, and that one of the express provisions of that treaty is that any neutral Hellenic state may join whichever side it chooses. It is intolerable that Corinth should be allowed to draw men for her navy not only from her allies but from the rest of Hellas, with no small number coming from your own subjects, while we are excluded both from the alliance left open to us by treaty and from any help we might get from elsewhere—and that you should be accused of political immorality if you grant our request. We have far greater grounds to complain of you if you refuse: if we, who are in danger and are no enemies of yours, meet with rebuff at your hands, while Corinth, the aggressor and your enemy, not only meets no hindrance from you but is even allowed to draw material for war from your dependencies. This must not be. Either forbid her enlisting men in your dominions, or send us too whatever help you think advisable.

“But your real policy is to give us avowed support. The advantages of this course, as we said at the beginning, are many. We mention one that is perhaps the chief. Could there be a clearer guarantee of our good faith than the fact that the power at enmity with you is also at enmity with us, and that this power is fully able to punish defection? And there is a wide difference between declining the alliance of an inland power and that of a maritime one. Your first aim should be to prevent, if possible, the existence of any naval power except your own; failing this, to secure the friendship of the strongest that does exist. If any of you believe that what we urge is expedient but fear to act on it for fear of breaking the treaty, remember this: whatever your fears, your strength will be formidable to your enemies; and whatever your confidence in refusing us, your weakness will hold no terrors for a strong enemy. Remember too that your decision is for Athens no less than for Corcyra, and that you are not making the best provision for her interests if, at a time when you anxiously scan the horizon for the war that is all but upon you, you hesitate to attach to your side a place whose adhesion or estrangement carries the most vital consequences. For Corcyra lies conveniently on the coast-route to Italy and Sicily, able to bar naval reinforcements from there to the Peloponnese, and from the Peloponnese to there; and in other respects too she is a most desirable station. To sum up as briefly as possible, weighing both general and particular considerations, see the folly of sacrificing us. Remember there are only three considerable naval powers in Hellas—Athens, Corcyra, and Corinth—and that if you let two of these three become one, with Corinth getting us for herself, you will have to hold the sea against the combined fleets of Corcyra and the Peloponnese. But if you receive us, you will have our ships to reinforce you in the struggle.”
Such were the words of the Corcyraeans. After they had finished, the Corinthians spoke as follows:

“These Corcyraeans in the speech we have just heard do not confine themselves to the question of their reception into your alliance. They also accuse us of injustice and claim to be the victims of an unjustifiable war. We must touch on both these points before we proceed to the rest of what we have to say, so that you may have a more accurate view of the grounds of our claim, and good reason to reject their petition. According to them, their old policy of refusing all offers of alliance was a policy of moderation. In fact it was adopted for bad ends, not good ones; their conduct is such that they have no wish for allies present to witness it, nor do they want the shame of asking for their concurrence. Besides, their geographical position makes them independent of others, so that decisions in cases where they injure anyone lie not with judges chosen by mutual agreement but with themselves: they rarely sail to their neighbours, while foreign vessels are constantly forced to put in at Corcyra. In short, the object of their specious policy of complete isolation is not to avoid sharing in the crimes of others, but to secure a monopoly of crime for themselves—the licence of outrage wherever they can compel it, of fraud wherever they can elude detection, and the enjoyment of their gains without shame. If they were the honest men they pretend to be, the less hold others had on them, the more clearly they could have shown their honesty by giving and taking what was just.

“But such has not been their conduct, either toward others or toward us. The attitude of our colony toward us has always been one of estrangement, and is now one of hostility. ‘We were not sent out,’ they say, ‘to be ill-treated.’ We answer that we did not found the colony to be insulted by them, but to be their head and to be regarded with proper respect. Our other colonies honour us, and we are much loved by our colonists; clearly, if the majority are satisfied with us, these can have no good reason for a dissatisfaction in which they stand alone. We are not acting improperly in making war on them, nor are we doing so without grave provocation. Besides, even if we were in the wrong, it would be honourable in them to give way to our wishes, and disgraceful for us to trample on their moderation. But in the pride and licence of wealth they have sinned against us again and again, and never more deeply than when Epidamnus, our dependency, which they made no move to claim in its distress until we came to its relief, was seized by them and is now held by force of arms.

“As for their claim that they wished the question to be submitted first to arbitration, it is obvious that a challenge from a party safe in a commanding position cannot earn the credit due only to the man who, before resorting to arms, places himself on a level with his adversary in deeds as well as in words. In their case, it was not before they laid siege to the place, but only after they finally understood that we would not tamely suffer it, that they hit on the specious word ‘arbitration.’ Not satisfied with their misconduct there, they appear here now demanding that you join them not in alliance but in crime, and receive them despite their being at war with us. They should have made their overtures to you when they stood firmest, not at a time when we are wronged and they are in danger; not at a time when you would be admitting to a share in your protection those who never admitted you to a share in their power, and would be incurring an equal share of blame from us with those whose offences you had no hand in. They should have shared their power with you before asking you to share your fortunes with them.

“So the reality of the grievances we come to complain of, and the violence and rapacity of our opponents, have both been proved. But that you cannot fairly receive them—this you have still to learn. It may be true that one provision of the treaty is that any state whose name was not on the list may join whichever side it pleases. But this agreement is not meant for those whose object in joining is to harm other powers, but for those whose need of support does not arise from defection, and whose adhesion will not bring war instead of peace to the power mad enough to receive them—which is what will happen to you if you do not listen to us. For you cannot become their auxiliary and remain our friend; if you join in their attack, you must share the punishment which the defenders inflict on them. You have the best possible right to be neutral, or, failing that, you should on the contrary join us against them. Corinth at least has a treaty with you; with Corcyra you have never even had a truce. But do not lay down the principle that defection is to be patronised. When the Samians revolted from you, did we cast our vote against you, when the rest of the Peloponnesian powers were equally divided on whether to assist them? No. We told them to their face that every power has the right to punish its own allies. If you make it your policy to receive and assist all offenders, you will find that just as many of your dependencies will come over to us, and the principle you establish will press less heavily on us than on yourselves.

“This, then, is what Hellenic law entitles us to demand as a right. But we also have advice to offer and claims on your gratitude—claims that, since there is no danger of our injuring you (as we are not enemies) and since our friendship does not amount to very frequent dealings, ought to be settled at the present juncture. When you needed warships for the war against the Aeginetans, before the Persian invasion, Corinth supplied you with twenty vessels. That good turn, and the line we took on the Samian question, when we were the cause of the Peloponnesians refusing to assist them, allowed you to conquer Aegina and to punish Samos. We acted thus at moments when, if ever, men forget everything for the sake of victory against their enemies—regarding any man who helps them then as a friend, even if he has been a foe up to that moment, and any man who opposes them then as a foe, even if he has been a friend; indeed, they let their real interests suffer because of their absorbing preoccupation with the struggle.

“Weigh these considerations carefully. Let your young men learn what they are from their elders, and let them resolve to do unto us as we have done unto you. Do not acknowledge the justice of what we say only to dispute its wisdom in the event of war. Generally speaking, the straightest path is the wisest; and the war that the Corcyraeans have used as a bugbear to persuade you to do wrong is still uncertain, and not worth being carried away by into the instant and declared enmity of Corinth. It would be wiser to try to undo the unfavourable impression your conduct toward Megara has created. A kindness shown at the right moment has a greater power to remove old grievances than the facts of the case may warrant. Do not be seduced by the prospect of a great naval alliance. Refraining from injustice toward other first-rate powers is a greater tower of strength than anything to be gained by sacrificing lasting tranquility for an apparent short-term advantage. It is now our turn to benefit by the principle we laid down at Lacedaemon, that every power has the right to punish her own allies. We claim the same from you, and protest against your rewarding our vote on your behalf by injuring us with yours. On the contrary, return us like for like, remembering that this is the very crisis in which the man who lends aid is most a friend, and the man who opposes is most a foe. As for these Corcyraeans—neither receive them into alliance against our wishes, nor be their abettors in crime. Do this, and you will act as we have a right to expect of you, and at the same time best serve your own interests.”
Such were the words of the Corinthians.

When the Athenians had heard both sides, two assemblies were held. In the first, public feeling was clearly inclined to listen to Corinth. In the second, the mood had shifted, and an alliance with Corcyra was decided on, with certain reservations. It was to be a defensive, not an offensive alliance. It would not violate the treaty with the Peloponnese: Athens could not be required to join Corcyra in any attack on Corinth. But each of the contracting parties had a right to the other’s help against invasion, whether of its own territory or of an ally’s. It was now beginning to be felt that the coming of the Peloponnesian war was only a matter of time, and no one wanted to see a naval power as great as Corcyra sacrificed to Corinth. Yet if the two could be left to weaken each other by mutual conflict, that would be useful preparation for the struggle Athens might one day have to wage with Corinth and the other naval powers. At the same time the island lay conveniently on the coastal passage to Italy and Sicily. With these views Athens received Corcyra into alliance and, soon after the Corinthians had departed, sent ten ships to her assistance. They were commanded by Lacedaemonius, son of Cimon, Diotimus, son of Strombichus, and Proteas, son of Epicles. Their instructions were to avoid collision with the Corinthian fleet except under certain circumstances. If it sailed to Corcyra and threatened a landing on her coast or any of her possessions, they were to do their utmost to prevent it. These instructions came from a wish to avoid breaking the treaty.

Meanwhile the Corinthians completed their preparations and sailed for Corcyra with one hundred and fifty ships. Of these Elis furnished ten, Megara twelve, Leucas ten, Ambracia twenty-seven, Anactorium one, and Corinth herself ninety. Each contingent had its own admiral, the Corinthian commander being Xenoclides, son of Euthycles, with four colleagues. Sailing from Leucas, they made land on the part of the continent opposite Corcyra. They anchored in the harbour of Chimerium, in Thesprotis. Above it, at some distance from the sea, lies the city of Ephyre, in the Elean district. Near this city the Acherusian lake pours its waters into the sea. The lake gets its name from the river Acheron, which flows through Thesprotis and falls into it. The river Thyamis also flows there, forming the boundary between Thesprotis and Kestrine; between these rivers rises the point of Chimerium. In this part of the continent the Corinthians now anchored and formed an encampment. When the Corcyraeans saw them coming, they manned one hundred and ten ships, commanded by Meikiades, Aisimides, and Eurybatus, and stationed themselves at one of the Sybota islands; the ten Athenian ships were present. On Point Leukimme they posted their land forces and one thousand heavy infantry who had come from Zacynthus to help. The Corinthians on the mainland had allies of their own. The barbarians flocked in large numbers to their assistance, the inhabitants of this part of the continent being old allies of theirs.

When the Corinthian preparations were complete, they took three days’ provisions and put out from Chimerium by night, ready for action. Sailing at dawn, they sighted the Corcyraean fleet out at sea coming toward them. As soon as the two sides saw each other, they formed in order of battle. On the Corcyraean right wing lay the Athenian ships; the rest of the line was held by Corcyraean vessels formed in three squadrons, each commanded by one of the three admirals. Such was the Corcyraean formation. The Corinthian was as follows: on the right wing lay the Megarian and Ambraciot ships; in the centre, the rest of the allies in order; the left was made up of the best sailers in the Corinthian navy, to face the Athenians and the right wing of the Corcyraeans. As soon as the signals went up on either side, they joined battle. Both sides had a large number of heavy infantry on their decks, and many archers and javelin-throwers, the old, imperfect armament still prevailing. The sea-fight was stubborn but not remarkable for its skill; it was more like a battle on land. Whenever the ships charged, the crowd and crush of vessels made it impossible to disengage easily; besides, both sides relied chiefly on the heavy infantry on the decks, who stood and fought in order while the ships remained stationary. The manoeuvre of breaking the line was not attempted; in short, strength and pluck had more share in the fight than skill. Tumult reigned everywhere, the battle one scene of confusion. Meanwhile the Athenian ships, by coming up to the Corcyraeans whenever they were pressed, alarmed the enemy, though their commanders could not actually join the fight for fear of breaking their orders. The right wing of the Corinthians suffered most. The Corcyraeans routed it, chased its ships in disorder to the continent with twenty of their own vessels, sailed up to the Corinthian camp, burned the empty tents, and plundered the supplies. So in this quarter the Corinthians and their allies were defeated and the Corcyraeans victorious. But where the Corinthians themselves stood, on the left, they had a clear success; the already small Corcyraean force was further weakened by the absence of the twenty ships that had gone in pursuit. Seeing the Corcyraeans hard pressed, the Athenians at last began to assist them more openly. At first they refrained from charging any ships; but as the rout became obvious and the Corinthians pressed on, the moment came when everyone joined in, all distinctions were abandoned, and it came to this: the Corinthians and Athenians raised their hands against each other.

After the rout the Corinthians, instead of lashing fast and towing off the hulls of the vessels they had disabled, turned their attention to the men, butchering them as they sailed through, more interested in killing than in taking prisoners. They even slew some of their own friends by mistake, not knowing that the right wing had been defeated. The number of ships on both sides, and the distance over which they covered the sea, made it hard, once the lines had joined, to tell the conquering ships from the conquered. This battle was far greater than any before it, at least between Hellenes, in the number of vessels engaged. After they had chased the Corcyraeans to land, the Corinthians turned to the wrecks and their dead, most of whom they managed to recover and convey to Sybota, the rendezvous of the land forces furnished by their barbarian allies. Sybota, it should be noted, is a deserted harbour in Thesprotis. This task done, they re-formed and sailed against the Corcyraeans, who advanced to meet them with all the ships still fit for service, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, fearing that they might attempt a landing on their territory. It was getting late, and the paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water. They had spotted twenty Athenian ships sailing up. These had been sent out afterwards to reinforce the original ten by the Athenians, who feared—as it turned out, justly—the defeat of the Corcyraeans and the inability of so few ships to protect them. The Corinthians saw these ships first. They suspected they were from Athens, and that what they saw was not all but that more were behind, so they began to retire. The Corcyraeans had not yet sighted them, since they were advancing from a point harder for them to see, and were wondering why the Corinthians were backing water, when some of them caught sight of the ships and cried out that there were sails in view ahead. At that they too withdrew, for it was now getting dark, and the retreat of the Corinthians had ended hostilities. So the two sides parted, and the battle ceased with night. The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme when these twenty Athenian ships, under the command of Glaucon, son of Leagrus, and Andocides, son of Leogoras, made their way through the corpses and the wrecks and sailed up to the camp not long after they were sighted. It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared they might be hostile vessels; but they soon recognised them, and the ships came to anchor.

The next day the thirty Athenian vessels put out to sea, accompanied by all the Corcyraean ships still seaworthy, and sailed to the harbour at Sybota, where the Corinthians lay, to see if they would engage. The Corinthians put out from the land and formed a line in the open sea, but went no further, having no intention of taking the offensive. They saw fresh reinforcements arrived from Athens, and they faced numerous difficulties of their own: the need to guard the prisoners on board, and the lack of any means of refitting their ships in a deserted place. They were thinking more about how to make their voyage home; they feared that the Athenians might consider the treaty broken by the recent collision and forbid their departure.

So they decided to put some men on board a boat and send them, without a herald’s wand, to the Athenians, as an experiment. They spoke as follows: “You do wrong, Athenians, to begin war and break the treaty. We are engaged in punishing our enemies, and we find you placing yourselves in our path in arms against us. If your intentions are to prevent us sailing to Corcyra, or anywhere else we may wish, and if you are determined to break the treaty, then take us first—we who are here—and treat us as enemies.” That was what they said, and the whole Corcyraean force within hearing immediately called out to seize them and kill them. But the Athenians answered as follows: “We are neither beginning war, Peloponnesians, nor breaking the treaty. These Corcyraeans are our allies, and we have come to help them. So if you want to sail anywhere else, we put no obstacle in your way; but if you sail against Corcyra, or any of her possessions, we shall do our best to stop you.”

On receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians began preparations for the voyage home and set up a trophy at Sybota on the continent; the Corcyraeans took up the wrecks and dead that had been carried out to them by the current and by a wind that rose in the night and scattered them in all directions, and set up their own trophy at Sybota on the island, as victors. The reasons each side had for claiming the victory were these. The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night; they had thus been able to recover most of the wrecks and dead, and they held no fewer than a thousand prisoners of war and had sunk close to seventy vessels. The Corcyraeans had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the arrival of the Athenians had recovered the wrecks and dead on their own side. They had also seen the Corinthians retreat before them, backing water at the sight of the Athenian ships, and, after the Athenians’ arrival, refuse to sail out against them from Sybota. Both sides therefore claimed the victory.

On the voyage home the Corinthians took Anactorium, which stands at the mouth of the Ambracian gulf. The place was taken by treachery; it was common ground to the Corcyraeans and Corinthians. After establishing Corinthian settlers there, they returned home. Eight hundred of the Corcyraeans were slaves, and these they sold; two hundred and fifty they kept in captivity and treated with great care, in the hope that they might bring their country over to Corinth on their return—most of them being, as it happened, men of very high standing in Corcyra. Thus Corcyra maintained her political existence in the war with Corinth, and the Athenian vessels left the island. This was the first cause of the war that Corinth had against the Athenians: that they had fought against Corinth alongside the Corcyraeans during a time of treaty.

Almost immediately after this, fresh disputes arose between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians and contributed their share to the war. Corinth was making schemes for revenge, and Athens suspected her hostility. The Potidæans, who inhabit the isthmus of Pallene, being a Corinthian colony but tributary allies of Athens, were ordered to raze the wall facing Pallene, give hostages, dismiss the Corinthian magistrates, and refuse in future to receive the men sent annually from Corinth to succeed them. It was feared that they might be persuaded by Perdiccas and the Corinthians to revolt, and might draw the rest of the allies in the direction of Thrace into revolt with them. These precautions against the Potidæans were taken by the Athenians immediately after the battle at Corcyra. Not only was Corinth at last openly hostile, but Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, had been turned from an old friend and ally into an enemy. He had become an enemy because the Athenians had entered into alliance with his brother Philip and with Derdas, who were leagued against him. In his alarm he had sent to Lacedaemon to try to involve the Athenians in war with the Peloponnesians, and was trying to win over Corinth in order to bring about the revolt of Potidæa. He also made overtures to the Chalcidians toward Thrace, and to the Bottiaeans, urging them to join in the revolt, for he thought that if these places on the border could be made his allies, the war would be easier to wage with their cooperation. Aware of all this and wanting to forestall the revolt of the cities, the Athenians acted as follows. They were just then sending off thirty ships and a thousand heavy infantry for his country under the command of Archestratus, son of Lycomedes, with four colleagues. They instructed the captains to take hostages from the Potidæans, raze the wall, and be on guard against the revolt of the neighbouring cities.

Meanwhile the Potidæans sent envoys to Athens on the chance of persuading them to take no new steps in their affairs; they also went to Lacedaemon, with the Corinthians, to secure support in case of need. After prolonged negotiation they failed to obtain anything satisfactory from the Athenians—they could not, for all their efforts, prevent the vessels destined for Macedonia from also sailing against them. But they received from the Lacedaemonian government a promise to invade Attica if the Athenians attacked Potidæa. Favoured by the moment, the Potidæans at last entered into league with the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans and revolted. Perdiccas persuaded the Chalcidians to abandon and demolish their towns on the seaboard and to settle inland at Olynthus, making that one city a strong place. To those who followed his advice he gave a part of his territory in Mygdonia, around Lake Bolbe, as a place to live while the war against the Athenians lasted. They duly demolished their towns, moved inland, and prepared for war. The thirty Athenian ships, arriving in the Thracian region, found Potidæa and the rest already in revolt. Their commanders, judging it impossible with their present force to wage war on Perdiccas and on the confederate towns at the same time, turned to Macedonia, their original destination, and once established there carried on the war alongside Philip and the brothers of Derdas, who had invaded the country from the interior.

Meanwhile the Corinthians, with Potidæa in revolt and the Athenian ships on the coast of Macedonia, alarmed for the safety of the place and feeling its danger as their own, sent volunteers from Corinth and mercenaries from the rest of the Peloponnese—sixteen hundred heavy infantry in all, and four hundred light troops. Aristeus, son of Adimantus, who was always a steady friend of the Potidæans, took command of the expedition; it was largely out of love for him that most of the men from Corinth volunteered. They reached Thrace forty days after the revolt of Potidæa.

The Athenians too immediately received news of the revolt of the cities. On learning that Aristeus and his reinforcements were on their way, they sent two thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens and forty ships against the rebellious places, under the command of Callias, son of Calliades, with four colleagues. They reached Macedonia first and found the force of a thousand men sent out earlier just become masters of Therme and besieging Pydna. They joined the siege and besieged Pydna for a time. They later came to terms and concluded a forced alliance with Perdiccas, hastened by the calls of Potidæa and by the arrival of Aristeus there. They withdrew from Macedonia, going to Beroea and from there to Strepsa. After a futile attempt on Strepsa, they pressed on by land to Potidæa with three thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens, besides a number of allies and six hundred Macedonian horsemen, the followers of Philip and Pausanias. With them sailed seventy ships along the coast. Advancing by short marches, on the third day they reached Gigonus and encamped there.

Meanwhile the Potidæans and the Peloponnesians under Aristeus were encamped on the side facing Olynthus, on the isthmus, awaiting the Athenians, with their market set up outside the city. The allies had made Aristeus general of all the infantry, while command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas, who had at once left the Athenian alliance and gone back to that of the Potidæans, deputing Iolaus as his general. The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus and await the Athenian attack, leaving the Chalcidians and the allies outside the isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry from Perdiccas in Olynthus, to fall on the Athenian rear when they advanced against him—putting the enemy between two fires. Callias, the Athenian general, and his colleagues sent the Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus to prevent any movement from that quarter. The Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched against Potidæa. When they reached the isthmus and saw the enemy preparing for battle, they formed against him, and the engagement followed soon after. The wing of Aristeus, with the Corinthians and other picked troops around him, routed the wing opposed to it and pursued for a considerable distance. But the rest of the Potidæan and Peloponnesian army was defeated by the Athenians and took refuge inside the fortifications. Returning from the pursuit, Aristeus saw the defeat of the rest of the army. At a loss which of the two risks to take—going to Olynthus or to Potidæa—he finally decided to draw his men into as small a space as possible and force his way at a run into Potidæa. Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he passed along the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe, though a few were lost. Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidæans from Olynthus, which is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidæa, when the battle began and the signals went up, advanced a little way to help; the Macedonian horse formed against them to prevent it. But when victory quickly declared for the Athenians and the signals were taken down, they retired back behind the wall, and the Macedonians returned to the Athenians. So no cavalry was present on either side. After the battle the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back the dead to the Potidæans under truce. The Potidæans and their allies had close to three hundred killed; the Athenians, one hundred and fifty of their own citizens, including their general, Callias.

Siege-works were now raised and manned by the Athenians on the isthmus side of the wall. On the Pallene side none were raised. They did not feel strong enough at once to keep a garrison on the isthmus and cross over to Pallene to raise works there; they feared that the Potidæans and their allies might take advantage of their division to attack them. Meanwhile the Athenians at home, learning that there were no works on the Pallene side, some time later sent out sixteen hundred heavy infantry of their own citizens under the command of Phormio, son of Asopius. On reaching Pallene he fixed his headquarters at Aphytis and led his army against Potidæa by short marches, ravaging the country as he advanced. Since no one ventured to meet him in the field, he raised works against the wall on the Pallene side. So at last Potidæa was strongly invested on both sides, and from the sea by the ships cooperating in the blockade. Aristeus, seeing the investment complete and having no hope of saving the place except in the event of some movement from the Peloponnese, or some other improbable contingency, advised that all but five hundred men should watch for a wind and sail out of the place, so that provisions might last longer. He was willing to remain himself among those who stayed. Unable to persuade them, and wishing to take the next best course and have things outside in the best possible state, he eluded the Athenian guardships and sailed out. Remaining with the Chalcidians, he carried on the war: in particular he laid an ambush near the city of the Sermylians and cut off many of them; he also communicated with the Peloponnese and tried to contrive some method of bringing help. Meanwhile, after the investment of Potidæa was complete, Phormio used his sixteen hundred men to ravage Chalcidice and Bottica, and took some of the towns.
